prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as my single prize part, and the round-1 exchange sharpened rather than weakened my reasons. The achievement is one idea followed by one demonstration of performance: trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength cancels the light shift, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated without perturbing the transition, and fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 have followed. As an experimentalist I ask first what was measured and who else reproduced it. Here the answer is numerical agreement between clocks built independently in Japan, the US, France, Germany and China, with comparisons that are routine. That is a stricter form of reproducibility than any other entry on the list can show. The credit of Katori for the concept and first Sr lattice clock and Ye for taking accuracy and stability to the record regime is compact and maps onto the two things that were actually done. I have dropped the redefinition of the second as an argument for timing; Lindroth is right that a prize should rest on what has been demonstrated. Having tried the common standard the chair asks for (independent confirmation, and how much the result depends on the individual sample or device), B026 meets it more fully today than B033, though I accept that B033 opens a new regime of physics and that is a different virtue.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize is the real risk: to a reader outside atomic physics this can look like the third prize for optical precision metrology. It also lacks the discovery narrative of moire graphene, and I must admit that six of eight colleagues weigh that narrative more heavily than I do. Lattice-clock contributors beyond Katori and Ye (Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Derevianko on theory) are left aside by a two-name credit, and my own recollection of first-demonstration priority has not been checked. Finally, the practical payoffs (geodesy, constants, dark matter) are promising but not delivered.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether the earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes make the optical lattice clock look incremental to the wider Academy, and keeps B026 as first alternative if B033 is blocked on credit.
responses.response: I take the question seriously and answer it on physics. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a ruler that links optical and microwave frequencies, and 2012 recognised control of a single ion. Neither addresses the problem lattice clocks solve: a single ion gives accuracy but very poor signal-to-noise per unit time, while uncorrelated neutral atoms in free space suffer Doppler and recoil shifts. The magic wavelength lets one confine many atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime with the trap shift cancelled, which changes stability by orders of magnitude. The citation should therefore be drawn around the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation, not around clocks generally. Your point that B026 is the natural fallback if B033 stalls on the third seat matters to me, because it is exactly why I am keeping B033 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth argues the lattice clock is a new physical idea and not a larger version of the earlier work, and that the pending SI redefinition should not be cited as a reason for timing.
responses.response: I accept the second point and have removed the redefinition from my case; in round 1 I leaned on it too much. On the first point I agree with the substance and have written my citation to reflect it. Where I would add caution to your view is that the committee should not lean on field familiarity. We are both atomic physicists, so our enthusiasm is correlated, and I would rather have the condensed-matter members say plainly whether the magic-wavelength idea reads as new to them. Mehlig's remark that it is an elegant cancellation argument but a less surprising one than the graphene case is a fair reading, and I do not think it can be dismissed.

responses.point: Mehlig calls B026 the cleanest attribution with unquestionable maturity, but argues the discovery is an elegant extension of precision spectroscopy and that moire flat bands opened a regime that was previously unreachable, so B026 should not displace B033.
responses.response: I agree on attribution and maturity, and your point about the shared cancellation structure is a good one. I disagree on one thing: that the clock result is merely a recognised extension. The new thing is a measurement capability that did not exist, with a quantitative performance (1e-18) verified between laboratories, and that has already enabled relativistic geodesy at centimetre scale. On B033 itself, your own list of reservations (unsettled pairing mechanism, sample-to-sample variation, only about seven years of experiments) is a list of maturity issues, not of merit. I find those more serious than you do because I spend my time on devices whose behaviour depends on the sample. If the committee settles the Andrei question and tests the experimental claims against independent devices, I would find B033 a credible prize and say so on my ballot.

responses.point: Olsson regards B026 as the strongest fallback and, as an experimentalist, will not dismiss Andrei's pre-2018 STM record, while noting that the redefinition of the second is pending and the prize would partly reward an anticipated outcome.
responses.response: On the redefinition I have conceded the point to Lindroth and agree with you that it should not be a reason for the prize. The fact that independent clock comparisons already agree at the 1e-18 level means the case does not need it. I value your insistence on the Andrei record: the chair's first question, whether early STM flat-band evidence precedes the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction or only follows it, decides whether the third seat is Bistritzer or Andrei, and neither of us can settle it from memory. That uncertainty is a practical weight against B033 this year and a reason I would keep B026 as the lead, whereas for you it is a reason to keep B026 as a fallback.

responses.point: Eriksson finds the clock case strong on independent confirmation and invention but prefers B033 because moire graphene opened a field, and he is sceptical that the clocks can be paired with B033 under the three-laureate cap.
responses.response: I agree that a split prize is not feasible: B033 needs three names and the cap makes any pairing with B026 impossible, so these are competing configurations and not complementary ones. I also take your point on continuum-model idealisation, since lattice relaxation and strain changing the flat-band picture quantitatively is the same kind of device-level caveat I worry about. For the common standard the chair asks for, I would say a result earns a prize when independent groups with different devices obtain the same quantitative value. By that test the clock comparisons pass, and twisted graphene passes for the qualitative phase diagram but not yet for quantitative features, which is why I place it second and not first.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads lattice clocks as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I have argued it is, but the condensed-matter members and the Academy may not agree.
Whether the Andrei question for B033 resolves against Bistritzer; if it does, B033 weakens, and if it does not and the committee wants a discovery narrative, I would not oppose B033.
Fair treatment of lattice-clock contributors outside Katori and Ye, and the unverified first-demonstration priority between groups.
Whether applications such as geodesy and dark-matter searches will materialise at the scale suggested.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. I have no known direct tie to the Katori or Ye groups. My WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Johansson's Chalmers home, which bears on circuit-based candidates such as B010, which I do not prefer. Lund atomic physics works on laser spectroscopy and rare-earth-ion systems, which is adjacent to B037 and B039 but not a personal connection requiring recusal. As an atomic physicist I may be inclined to favour B026, and I flagged this in my response to Lindroth.
